title: Peaky load: priority windows and token fairness
summary: Customer runs a real-time inference platform with spiky traffic. Main goal: increase sustainable throughput during minute-scale spikes without blowing latency SLOs for high-priority flows. Discussed using time-windowed priority weights, dynamic max_num_seqs scaling, token caps per-request, and KV cache prewarm strategies. Agreed to run a 48h pilot with priority weighting enabled and a benchmark sheet to collect 95/99 latency and token cost impacts.
next_steps: Redwood to share priority-weighting config example and envoy route snippets (Maya) by 2026-04-16
Bluewave to paste recent traffic patterns and 2 days of production traces to the benchmark spreadsheet (Sarah) by 2026-04-17
SE to run a lab sim with their seq distribution and report P95/P99 tradeoffs (Owen) by 2026-04-20

Owen: Run simulated peaky-load bench with dynamic max_num_seqs (due 2026-04-20)

transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we got about an hour, so we'll try to focus on priority windows, max_num_seqs, and a couple related knobs. uh, quick intros?
[00:12] Sarah Nguyen: Sarah here, head of ML infra at Bluewave. we run a real-time analytics endpoint, pretty bursty, like small windows of high qps.
[00:20] Carlos Ruiz: Carlos, platform eng. mostly care about predictable tail latency and cost.
[00:26] Priya Desai: Priya, SRE. if we break SLAs the paging starts.
[00:30] Tom Becker: Tom from data science, interested in quality impact of quant.
[00:33] Maya Chen: Cool. Owen from our side?
[00:36] Owen Patel: Hey all, Owen SE. I'll dig into scheduler knobs and sim results.
[00:40] Maya Chen: Great. high-level problem: Bluewave has minute-scale spikes where many low-priority batch jobs and user-facing requests hit same pool; want to avoid head-of-line and keep premium flows below 200ms p95. we suggested using priority windows and token fairness — walk through a config.
[00:58] Sarah Nguyen: Right, the tricky bit is the spikes are sudden — sometimes 10x baseline for 30-90s — so continuous batching can help throughput but worsens tail for interactive requests.
[01:09] Owen Patel: Exactly. two levers we usually combine: dynamic max_num_seqs and priority-weighted batching. max_num_seqs sets the maximum number of concurrent sequences a worker will pack per token step. if you raise it you increase throughput but can hurt p99 latency for small, high-priority requests.
[01:30] Carlos Ruiz: Can you explain priority-weighted batching? we saw something about 'priority windows' in the docs but not concrete.
[01:36] Owen Patel: Sure. priority-weighted batching means the scheduler calculates a weight per priority class and builds batches respecting those weights. e.g., in a 100-slot batch with weight high=70, medium=20, low=10; high-priority gets most slots, so even if low floods, high still gets served quickly. windows are time buckets — you can change weights dynamically every 5s or 30s to respond to spikes.
[02:01] Priya Desai: Sounds promising. But what about fairness? if high gets 70% forever low never completes.
[02:07] Owen Patel: Right, that's where token fairness and decay come in. we recommend a credit-based system: each priority accrues credits when underutilized, decays when used. another simple knob is per-request token_cap — you can cap the tokens consumed by low-priority requests to avoid single request monopolizing a slot.
[02:26] Tom Becker: Token cap — doesn't that affect model responses? like longer answers get cut.
[02:30] Maya Chen: You can cap only on low-priority background tasks; for user-facing flows you keep higher caps. Also we have adaptive truncation: server-side can request a 'trim' token strategy where the model is asked to summarize rather than fully expand if hitting caps.
[02:45] Sarah Nguyen: OK, let's talk numbers. what's safe for max_num_seqs on A100-ish hosts? we run mixed models quantized to 4-bit.
[02:53] Owen Patel: For quantized Llama-variant at sequence lengths under 512, we've seen good sustained throughput at max_num_seqs of 18-24 on a single GPU with mixed batching and KV caching enabled. but those numbers assume warm KV caches; cold-cache throughput drops significantly because KV materialization per seq is expensive.
[03:13] Carlos Ruiz: So KV cache warmup strategy is critical. what do you recommend for prewarming?
[03:17] Owen Patel: A few approaches: proactive prewarm using synthetic prefixes derived from recent traffic, sticky routing so hot users are pinned to warmed workers, and background low-priority prewarm jobs that feed tokens to workers to populate KV.
[03:32] Sarah Nguyen: Sticky routing would need session affinity. we run in VPC on-prem, can we do that with your private deployment?
[03:38] Maya Chen: Yes — Private supports session affinity with consistent hashing across the runtime pool and route policies in the control plane. you can pin by customer_id or session_token. note though this can reduce effective load balancing during failures, so combine with fallback policies.
[03:51] Priya Desai: Any security caveats with KV prewarm? we can't leak customer data.
[03:54] Owen Patel: Important point — prewarm must use sanitized or synthetic prompts. we provide tooling to generate prefix buckets that mirror length and token distribution but contain no sensitive content. you can also prewarm with hashed ids or non-sensitive templates.
[04:07] Tom Becker: Back to priority windows, how often should we change weights? every 5s seems fine?
[04:12] Owen Patel: It depends on spike dynamics. for minute-scale spikes we found a 10-30s window hits a good balance: responsive enough to adapt, but not so fast that you thrash the scheduler. also you can tie windows to traffic signals — if you detect QPS delta > 3x then switch to 'spike' weight set for the next two windows.
[04:31] Sarah Nguyen: Can we do predictive prewarming? i.e., detect rising trends and prewarm before the burst hits.
[04:36] Owen Patel: Yes, we support trend-based alarms from your telemetry. integrate a short-timeseries model to forecast next 30s, then trigger prewarm and weight changes. we've shipped a reference app using EWMA of qps rate.
[04:49] Carlos Ruiz: On quantization: Tom asked about quality. we saw occasional hallucinations when switching from 8-bit to 4-bit in our offline tests.
[04:57] Tom Becker: Yeah, quality drop was subtle but meaningful for some prompts.
[05:02] Owen Patel: Quantization affects activations and numeric range; 4-bit with GPT-style models sometimes affects longer-context coherence. for throughput you can run 4-bit for low-priority inference and 8-bit or fp16 for high-priority. Redwood runtime supports model variant fallbacks per-request (costly but mitigates quality regressions).
[05:20] Priya Desai: How's the fallback implemented? do we pay double?
[05:24] Owen Patel: It's an on-demand pull. you can configure automatic fallback if p95 exceeded or if quality check fails. cost impact depends on how often you trigger fallback. we surface token delta and estimated $ impact in the console for any rollout.
[05:36] Sarah Nguyen: Can we measure quality regressions in the pilot? like automated evals using our prompt set?
[05:40] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Redwood Optimize can run evals during pilot with your prompt set and compare variants. we'll link the eval harness in the next email.
[05:48] Carlos Ruiz: backpressure — during spikes how do we avoid overload? we prefer graceful degradation over queueing up huge backlogs.
[05:55] Owen Patel: A few things: token bucket at ingress, immediate drop for requests exceeding per-client token cap, rate-shedding for low-priority classes, and queue-time SLO enforced by rejecting when estimated schedule delay > X ms. you can also set max inflight per-client.
[06:12] Tom Becker: Is there a way to ensure a minimum throughput for background jobs without affecting interactive latency?
[06:16] Owen Patel: Yes: reserve a small dedicated slot pool or set a minimum guaranteed weight for low-priority so they get a steady trickle; combine with longer batch windows for them so they pare down latency effect on high-priority.
[06:28] Priya Desai: We care about p99 more than p95 for some endpoints. when you tune max_num_seqs, is there an automated search?
[06:35] Owen Patel: We have a guided profiler that runs a binary search across max_num_seqs and measures p95/p99 vs tokens/sec. It suggests an operating point given a tail latency SLO and desired cost target. It will also test with cold and warm KV cache and report sensitivity.
[06:48] Sarah Nguyen: Let's look at a hypothetical: baseline p95 is 160ms, p99 is 420ms. if we increase max_num_seqs from 8 to 20, what's typical impact?
[06:58] Owen Patel: In our labs: p95 might change from 160ms->190ms but tokens/sec increases 2.4x. p99 can jump more — maybe 420ms->900ms if KV cache cold or if there's a single long request blocking. With priority weighting, high-priority p99 stays closer to target because they get reserved slots.
[07:18] Maya Chen: note those numbers vary with model, seq length, and quant. this is why the pilot and sims are necessary.
[07:24] Carlos Ruiz: You mentioned token fairness. how's that enforced across multi-tenant workloads?
[07:29] Owen Patel: Typically with per-tenant token budgets and dynamic decay. each tenant has a moving window of tokens consumed; if a tenant exceeds budget we throttle them to low-priority for the remainder of window. Combined with priority weights, it prevents one noisy tenant from washing out others.
[07:46] Priya Desai: Are there observability hooks we can export to our prometheus Grafana stack?
[07:50] Maya Chen: Yes — per-route metrics (tokens/sec, kv_hitrate, batch_size_distribution, scheduler_wait_ms, queue_depth) and evictions. We'll also expose priority-specific metrics so you can see how weights affect latency.
[08:01] Tom Becker: We run private deployment in our VPC. any differences in knob behavior vs hosted?
[08:06] Owen Patel: Runtime behavior is the same. differences are in network egress, routing controls, and where the prewarm artifacts live. on private you control the KMS keys, and you can set stricter RBAC for who flips priority weights. also on private you can tune kernel selection per-GPU if you compile custom operators.
[08:22] Sarah Nguyen: Can we compile with our own kernels? we have some proprietary optimizations.
[08:26] Maya Chen: For enterprise private customers we can support custom kernel bundles but it's a more involved onboarding (compatibility testing). we can surface a plugin mechanism.
[08:34] Carlos Ruiz: Any gotchas on autoscaling? we autoscale nodes on CPU metrics today but not GPU. during spikes scale-up latency kills us.
[08:41] Owen Patel: For inference, scale-up latency is crucial. recommended: keep a small warm buffer of spare GPUs (burst pool) and use fast provisioning images. Also use horizontal autoscaler triggered on model-specific metrics like queue_depth or estimated schedule_delay rather than raw CPU.
[08:57] Sarah Nguyen: ok, let's brainstorm a pilot target configuration.
[09:00] Owen Patel: Proposed: two priority classes (interactive, background). weight set normal: interactive=80, background=20; spike weight set: interactive=90, background=10. max_num_seqs baseline=10, spike mode max_num_seqs=20 for background-only batches. token_cap background=256, interactive=2048. prewarm: synthetic prefixes from last 2 hours, run during ramp-up. windows: 20s.
[09:28] Carlos Ruiz: For the spike mode, you suggest raising max_num_seqs. won't that harm interactive latency?
[09:33] Owen Patel: The idea is to apply higher max_num_seqs primarily to background batching workers (i.e., workers marked as background), or use per-priority max_num_seqs. The scheduler supports per-priority max_num_seqs. so interactive workers remain at 10 while background can go to 20.
[09:48] Priya Desai: How do we partition workers? static pools?
[09:51] Owen Patel: Options: static pool labels, or dynamic eviction where the controller reassigns worker labels on detected patterns. static is simplest initially. dynamic can be risky if orchestration lags.
[09:59] Tom Becker: Let's discuss measurement: what logs should we collect during the pilot?
[10:03] Maya Chen: P95/P99 latency per-priority, batch size histogram, kv_hitrate, scheduler_wait, tokens_per_request, fail/reject counts, and resource utilization per-GPU. Also capture traces for a sample of interactive requests to see queuing vs execute time.
[10:18] Sarah Nguyen: We'll add success criteria: interactive p95 <200ms, interactive p99 <600ms, background throughput increases by 2x without starvation. If we meet those, we'll consider expansion to other endpoints.
[10:30] Carlos Ruiz: Small question: if a background request is halfway through and we change weights mid-window, is it preempted?
[10:36] Owen Patel: In-flight requests complete; weights affect batch composition for subsequent steps. you can configure immediate mode (start new windows immediately) or graceful mode (apply next window only to new sequences). immediate can cause jitter but is faster to adapt. graceful is more stable.
[10:50] Priya Desai: About per-client token budgets — do you store in Redis? we want low latency check on ingress.
[10:56] Owen Patel: We use an in-memory shard per-runtime for speed and periodic reconciliation with a persistent store (e.g., Redis or dynamo). for private deployments you can point to your low-latency store.
[11:06] Sarah Nguyen: Any advice about testing quantization fallback logic? we saw some flakiness under load.
[11:10] Owen Patel: Test in 3 phases: offline A/B on dev dataset, then synthetic load bench, then small-scale canary in prod. instrument a quality gate that reroutes to higher-precision variant if evaluation metric drops. also add sampling of outputs for human review initially.
[11:24] Tom Becker: How do we minimize double-spend when fallback happens (i.e., request computed in 4-bit then re-run in 8-bit)?
[11:30] Owen Patel: Redwood supports a speculative execution mode: run a fast 4-bit pass and stream partial output; in parallel start an 8-bit run only if quality checks fail. that reduces perceived latency and cost in common cases. However, it's more resource intensive if many requests fall back.
[11:47] Carlos Ruiz: Do you have example envoy snippets for priority header passing? we operate with envoy and istio.
[11:52] Maya Chen: yes, will include in config bundle. basically attach x-priority and session-id headers and map to route clusters that label requests. we also provide a middleware to handle token_cap enforcement at ingress.
[12:03] Sarah Nguyen: On metrics — can we have alerts for kv_hitrate dropping below 60%? we rely on high hitrate for good throughput.
[12:09] Owen Patel: Absolutely. Default suggestion is alert at 65% for more conservative ops. We can include runbook steps: check prewarm jobs, check cache eviction thresholds, inspect workload shift for new prefixes.
[12:22] Priya Desai: What's common cause of low kv hitrate? new user base? model rollout?
[12:26] Owen Patel: Common causes: new prefixes (new users or new prompt formats), model version changes that change keying semantics, or aggressive cache eviction due to low max_cache_size. Also multi-tenant eviction when one tenant dominates memory.
[12:39] Tom Becker: Let's discuss eviction policies. LRU is default but sometimes recency is not best if some users are periodic but heavy.
[12:46] Owen Patel: We support LRU, LFU, and cost-aware eviction (evict sequences with lowest expected future reuse weighted by token length). cost-aware is heavier but gives better long-tail throughput for periodic workloads.
[12:58] Sarah Nguyen: Operationally, how transparent are evictions in logs? we need to trace when an eviction causes a p99 spike.
[13:03] Maya Chen: Eviction events are logged with tenant, key prefix, and reason. you can attach the last-access timestamp and approximate size. We also send eviction-rate metric per-tenant for alerting.
[13:15] Carlos Ruiz: For the pilot we want to try cost-aware eviction on background pool only.
[13:19] Owen Patel: That works. set eviction policy per-pool.
[13:22] Sarah Nguyen: Ok, let's recap concrete steps and timeline.
[13:25] Maya Chen: Recap: 1) Redwood shares priority-weight config example + envoy snippet (Maya) by 4/16. 2) Bluewave uploads two days of traces + list of critical interactive endpoints (Sarah) by 4/17. 3) Owen runs sim for max_num_seqs sweep and reports with P95/P99 tradeoffs (Owen) by 4/20. 4) Pilot kickoff 4/22 where we'll enable priority windows, token caps, KV prewarm in controlled pool.
[13:49] Sarah Nguyen: Agreed. Also include the eval harness for quality checks (Tom).
[13:53] Maya Chen: We'll include that in the package. We'll also add a sample Grafana dashboard JSON for quick import.
[13:59] Carlos Ruiz: Any closing notes on security? we need SOC2 type docs for the pilot.
[14:03] Maya Chen: We'll attach SOC2 and network segmentation docs. For private, KMS options and audit logs are available.
[14:10] Priya Desai: Sounds good. thanks all.
[14:13] Tom Becker: Thanks. looking forward to the bench results.
[14:16] Sarah Nguyen: Thanks everyone.
[14:18] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the bundle and calendar invite for kickoff.
[14:22] [call ended]
